title: Human Genome reference completion to sequencing-platform and cost transition
pressure: Finishing a first human reference sequence made genome-wide biology possible but did not make routine individual-genome sequencing economically or operationally tractable.
preExistingWorldModel: The Human Genome Project had scaled clone-based mapping and Sanger sequencing into a coordinated international production effort; sequence maps, public databases and large sequencing centers already existed.
candidateRoutes: convert reference sequencing infrastructure into population-scale reusable data resources
observationsAndInstruments: The HGP announced completion in April 2003 after a draft-to-finished production phase.
NHGRI estimated a hypothetical second high-quality reference genome at roughly tens of millions of dollars in 2003, while tracking continuing cost decline.
NHGRI launched the $1,000 Genome technology programme in 2004 to pursue orders-of-magnitude cost reduction rather than treating HGP completion as the end state.
The 1000 Genomes Project later exploited new sequencing platforms and public data release to move from one reference toward population variation.
decisiveTests: sequence accuracy and coverage at HGP completion
cost per genome and sequencing throughput over time
ability of new platforms to support population-scale sequencing and rapid public data release
technicalOrScientificTransition: The trajectory moved from a one-off international reference-construction programme toward a reusable sequencing/data production capability whose cost, throughput and public-data interfaces became first-class scientific infrastructure.
rivalsAndFailures: HGP completion did not itself solve affordable individual sequencing.
Continued incremental sequencing improvements competed with explicit investment in high-risk new technology.
diffusionAndScaling: The scientific value expanded through cheaper sequencing and shared reference/variation resources rather than by repeating the original HGP organizational form.
standardsAndInstitutions: International consortia, NHGRI funding, public-data release norms and database operators jointly sustained the transition.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Privacy, consent and interpretation remained separate constraints from raw sequencing capability.
secondOrderEffects: Cheaper sequencing enlarged the feasible study population and shifted bottlenecks toward data interpretation, study design and clinical validity.
sourceNativeSummary: A completed reference sequence became a platform only because sequencing technology, cost curves, shared data, institutional programmes and population resources continued to evolve after 2003.
